top_story: Three months after Tehran threatened regional escalation in response to Trump’s warning that the U.S. could destroy Iran’s power grid, Washington and Tehran moved on 17 June to formalize an MoU ending fighting and maritime blockades in the Gulf, marking a sharp de-escalatory turn in one of the region’s most dangerous arenas. The agreement reduces immediate risks to Gulf shipping, energy flows, and coastal populations that had been exposed to disruption and retaliatory strikes during the confrontation. That diplomatic shift stands in stark contrast to Gaza, where the death toll since the U.S.-brokered ceasefire has surpassed 1,000, underscoring that formal ceasefire frameworks are not translating into civilian protection. The regional picture is therefore one of selective stabilization: the Gulf is edging away from interstate escalation, while Gaza remains trapped in lethal insecurity despite nominal de-escalation.
